nameStory: This tiny acrobat earns its 'jumping mouse' name from its incredible ability to leap up to 3 feet in a single bound using its powerful hind legs and extra-long tail for balance. The 'woodland' part of its name reflects its preference for deep forest habitats, unlike its meadow-dwelling jumping mouse cousins who prefer open grasslands.
description: The Eastern Woodland Jumping Mouse is a small, kangaroo-like rodent about the size of a house mouse but built for Olympic-level jumping. It has disproportionately large hind feet, a tail nearly twice as long as its body, and rich golden-brown fur with a distinctive dark stripe down its back. These nocturnal forest acrobats spend most of the year in hibernation, emerging only during the warmer months to forage for seeds and insects.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Mouse-sized body (3-4 inches) with kangaroo proportions - enormous hind feet and a remarkably long tail that feels thin and wiry, often 5-6 inches long

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Rich golden-brown to orange-brown fur that feels soft and dense, with a distinctive dark brown or blackish stripe running down the center of the back from head to tail

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Distinctive hopping pattern with small front paw prints and much larger elongated hind prints, often with a thin line between prints from the dragging tail

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in spectacular bouncing leaps when startled, can jump 3 feet in one bound, and freezes motionless when sensing danger before exploding into action

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in cool, moist woodlands near streams or boggy areas, often where mossy logs and dense understory provide cover

habitat: Look for these forest gymnasts in cool, moist woodlands throughout New England's mountains and northern regions, especially near streams, springs, or boggy areas. They prefer dense understory with plenty of fallen logs, moss-covered rocks, and thick vegetation that provides cover from predators. You'll find them in both coniferous and mixed hardwood forests, particularly where the forest floor stays damp and rich with decomposing leaves.

seasonality.spring: Emerges from hibernation in late April or May when you might spot one hopping across forest trails at dusk. Fresh tracks may be visible in soft mud near woodland streams.
seasonality.summer: Most active period for foraging and breeding, though still rarely seen due to nocturnal habits. Look for their distinctive hopping tracks in sandy or muddy areas along forest streams.
seasonality.fall: Busy preparing for hibernation by late September, building up fat reserves. May occasionally be spotted during daylight hours as they forage intensively before winter.
seasonality.winter: In deep hibernation underground - you won't find any signs of activity during New England's cold months.

funFact: Woodland jumping mice are champion sleepers of the mammal world, hibernating for up to 8 months of the year - longer than bears! They can lower their body temperature to just above freezing and slow their heart rate to barely detectable levels during their marathon winter nap.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with regular house mice or white-footed mice, but the woodland jumping mouse's extremely long tail and golden coloring with dark back stripe make it unmistakable once you know what to look for. Remember: if it has a tail longer than its body and hops like a tiny kangaroo, you've found a jumping mouse!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mice,' jumping mice aren't closely related to true mice and belong to their own special family. They're actually more closely related to jerboas from desert regions, sharing that distinctive hopping lifestyle and long-tail-for-balance body plan.
compareHints: The woodland jumping mouse is the only member of its genus in North America, making it unique among jumping mice for its forest habitat preference. Unlike the meadow jumping mouse found in the same regions, it has richer, more golden fur, a more prominent dark back stripe, and exclusively seeks out woodland environments rather than open grasslands or field edges.
